title: Chapter 9: Debugging with AI: Reading Errors and Tracebacks
video_title: Python Chapter 9: Debugging with AI, Reading Errors and Tracebacks
summary: Asha's end-of-day report prints a wrong total with no error. Follow her as she learns the three kinds of bugs, reads a traceback from the bottom up, finds a hidden bug with print debugging and writes a debugging prompt with the code, the exact error, the expected result and the actual result. Then watch her handle a day with no sales with an AI assistant at all six stages, catching a check that let 0 through and a change she did not ask for.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define a bug, then the speed point, then the vague AI question.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **bug** is a mistake that makes a program stop or give a wrong result.
Every programmer writes bugs. Good programmers find them fast.
A vague question to an AI often gets a confident fix for the wrong problem.

segments.say: A bug is a mistake that makes a program stop, or give a wrong result. Every programmer writes bugs, every day.
And here is the AI part. A vague question, like my code is wrong, fix it, often gets a confident fix for the wrong problem.

scenes.title: The idea: three kinds of bugs
scenes.direction: Teach the three kinds with the table. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Three kinds of bugs
visual.label: The idea
rows: An error report; no line runs
Some output, then an error report
A wrong result and no error at all

segments.say: Bugs come in three kinds, and each one shows itself in a different way.
A syntax error means Python cannot read the file. So it runs nothing at all, not even the first print.
A runtime error happens while the program runs. Some lines print, then Python stops and prints a report.
A logic error is the sneakiest. The program finishes, with no message. But the result is wrong.

visual.question: A program prints two lines, then stops with an error report. Which kind of bug is it?
visual.explain: Some lines ran, then Python stopped: that is a runtime error.

segments.say: Quick check. A program prints two lines, then stops with an error report. Which kind of bug is it?

after.say: A. A runtime error. Some lines ran first, so Python could read the file.

items: Syntax error: nothing runs.
Runtime error: it stops partway.
Logic error: a wrong result, no message.

segments.say: Take a breather. Here is what you know so far.
Next, Asha meets each kind of bug in her report.

scenes.title: Step 1: A syntax error stops everything
scenes.direction: Show the file with the missing bracket, ask whether line 2 prints, then read the report.

visual.heading: Step 1: One missing bracket
visual.hidden_text: Predict what prints before the report appears.

segments.say: Step 1. Asha's report starts with three lines. Line 2 prints the heading. It is correct.
Line 4 prints the tea price. Look at its end: the closing bracket is missing.

ask.question: Line 2 is correct. Does it print before Python reports the error?

after.say: No. Nothing prints at all. Python reads the whole file before it runs any line, and it could not read line 4.
The report names the file and line 4. The marker points at the opening bracket, the one that was never closed.
The fix goes at the end of the line: a closing bracket.
These messages come from Python 3.12 and newer. Older versions word some of them differently.

scenes.title: Step 2: Read a traceback from the bottom up
scenes.direction: Predict which lines print before the crash. Then read the traceback from the bottom up, one line at a time. Then find the cause on an earlier line and show the fix.

visual.heading: Step 2: A crash partway
visual.hidden_text: Predict what prints before the report appears.

segments.say: Step 2. Line 3 asks how many cups of tea were sold. Remember Chapter 4: input always gives back text.
Line 4 prints the answer. Line 5 multiplies the cups by the tea price, 3.5.

ask.question: The user types 12. Which lines print before Python stops?

after.say: Lines 2, 3 and 4 run, so their output appears. Then Python stops at line 5.

visual.heading: Read it from the bottom up

segments.say: This report is called a traceback. Read it from the bottom up. The last line names the kind of error, a Type Error. A sequence is a value made of parts in order, like a string.
The two lines above show the code, and the markers point at the part that failed: cups times 3.5.
Above that: the file, and line 5.

And the first line says: most recent call last. It means the newest step is at the bottom. In programs this size, there is only one step. In Chapter 16, when you write functions, tracebacks grow longer.

visual.heading: The cause is on an earlier line

segments.say: Here is the key idea. The line Python names is where it noticed the problem. The cause can be earlier.
Line 3 stored the answer as text. So the fix is on line 3: int, around the input.
Now 12 cups cost 42.00.

scenes.title: Step 3: Spot a logic error
scenes.direction: Teach: work out the expected result first. Ask for the expected total, then reveal the wrong one.

visual.heading: Step 3: Add up three sales
visual.hidden_text: Work out the expected total first.

segments.say: Step 3. This loop adds up three sales. Line 2 starts the total at 0.
Line 3 makes three passes. Line 4 asks for the price of each sale. Line 5 adds to the total.
Before you run any program, work out the expected result by hand. Otherwise, a wrong answer looks fine.

ask.question: The user types 4.50, 6.00 and 3.50. What total should the program print?

after.say: It should print 14.00. But it prints 6.00!
No error, no crash. Only a wrong number. That is a logic error, and only your expected result caught it.

scenes.title: Step 4: Print debugging
scenes.direction: Teach print debugging with one debug line, ask what it shows after sale 1, reveal, find the cause, fix.

segments.say: Step 4. To find a hidden bug, print the values of your variables while the program runs. This is called print debugging.
Asha adds line 6 inside the loop. It shows sale, price and total on every pass. It starts with the word DEBUG, so she can find it and remove it later.
Line 5 runs before the debug line, so you see the total after it changes.

ask.question: On the first pass, sale is 1 and price is 4.5. What total does the DEBUG line show?

after.say: Total is 1. It should be 4.5.
Then 3, then 6. The total grows by the sale number, 1, 2 and 3, not by the price.
So line 5 adds sale, where it should add price.

segments.say: Asha changes line 5 to add price, and removes the debug line. The total is 14.00, exactly as expected.

scenes.title: Step 5: A debugging prompt that works
scenes.direction: Teach the four parts of the prompt, row by row, then the cause-first rule. Quiz, then a breather.

visual.heading: Step 5: Four parts of a debugging prompt
visual.label: Build it
rows: The whole program, or the lines around the problem
The full traceback, or "no error message"
What you wanted, worked out by hand

segments.say: Step 5. An AI cannot see your screen. So give it four things. The code, and the exact error. If there is none, say: no error message.
Then the expected result, worked out by hand, and the actual result. The difference points at the bug.
Then ask for the cause before the fix. A cause you understand teaches you something.

visual.question: Your program prints a wrong total and no error. Which parts of the prompt matter most?
options: The expected result and the actual result
visual.explain: With no error message, only the difference between expected and actual shows the bug.

segments.say: Quick check. Your program prints a wrong total, and no error. Which parts of the prompt matter most?

after.say: B. The expected result and the actual result. With no error message, their difference is the only clue.

items: Read a traceback from the bottom up.
The cause can be on an earlier line.
Print values to find a hidden bug.

segments.say: Breather. You have found and fixed three kinds of bugs. Now, the whole report.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the day report
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Connect each line to a fix from the steps, ask for the average line, reveal. Hand over to the zero-sales test.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the day report
visual.hidden_text: Predict the average before the output appears.
visual.note: The user will type: 3, then 4.50, 6.00 and 3.50

segments.say: Back to the mission. Line 2 prints the heading, and every bracket is closed. Line 3 converts the number of sales with int, the fix from step 2.
Line 4 starts the total at 0. Lines 5 to 7 add up each price: the fix from step 4. Range goes up to sales plus 1, so it asks once for each sale.
Line 8 divides the total by the number of sales, and lines 9 to 11 print the report, with two decimal places.

ask.question: The total is 14.00 and there are 3 sales. What does line 11 print?

after.say: Average, 4.67. 14 divided by 3 is 4.666 and more, and two decimal places round it to 4.67.

And the total is 14.00, the money Asha took. Mission complete! But Asha has one more test in mind. What happens on a day with no sales at all? She will find out, with an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one day with no sales
scenes.direction: Teach the structured prompt skill. One conversation per stage, all about 0 sales. Stage 3 plants the >= mistake, stage 4 catches it with a case list, stage 5 fixes it and re-runs every case, stage 6 catches an ignored instruction.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: the debugging prompt
visual.label: Before you start
items: Give the code, the exact error, the expected result and the actual result.
Ask for the cause before the fix.
Test every fix yourself. Never paste private data.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is the debugging prompt: the code, the exact error, the expected result, and the actual result.
Ask for the cause first. Then test every fix yourself. And the safety habits from Chapter 1 still apply.

visual.heading: Plan: a bug hunt, not a fix

messages.text: I am a beginner. My day report crashes when I type 0 sales. Do not fix anything yet and do not write code. Give me a short plan to find the cause.

1. Run it with 0 and copy the full traceback.
2. Read the last line: the kind of error.
3. Find the line number and the values used on that line.
4. Decide what the report should print for 0 sales.
5. Change one thing, then test 0 and the cases that already worked.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha types 0 sales, and the report crashes. Before any fix, she asks for a plan to find the cause. No code yet.
The AI gives five steps. Copy the traceback, and read its last line. Find the line and its values. Decide what 0 sales should print. Then test 0, and the cases that worked.

messages.text: Here is the error for 0 sales. My reading: the kind of error is ZeroDivisionError, it happened on line 8, and the cause is that sales is 0. Do not fix the code. Is my reading right?
Yes, all three points are right. The markers point at `total / sales`. Dividing by zero has no answer, so Python stops.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha follows the plan. She runs the report with 0, and reads the traceback herself.
She writes down her reading: a Zero Division Error, on line 8, because sales is 0. Then she asks the AI to check her reading, without fixing anything.
The AI agrees with all three points. Dividing by zero has no answer, so Python stops.

messages.text: Add a check so that 0 sales prints No sales today. instead of crashing. Change only what is needed. Tell me exactly what it prints for 0 sales.
Here is the check. For 0 sales, the report prints `No sales today.`

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for a check, so that 0 sales prints, No sales today. She asks what it prints for 0.
The AI adds an if before the average, and promises: no sales today. It sounds completely sure.
Look at line 8, and remember the boundary values from Chapter 6.

ask.question: The AI says 0 sales prints `No sales today.` Is it right?

after.say: No. Greater than or equal to 0 is true when sales is 0. So the program still reaches the division.

segments.say: Asha runs it with 0. The same crash, now on line 9. The AI's fix crashed on the same division.

messages.text: List test cases for my report, with the exact input and the expected last lines for each. Include 0 sales, 1 sale and 3 sales.

1. 0 sales: `No sales today.`
2. 1 sale of 5.00: Total 5.00, Average 5.00.
3. 3 sales of 4.50, 6.00 and 3.50: Total 14.00, Average 4.67.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks for test cases, each with the exact input and the expected result: 0 sales, 1 sale and 3 sales.
The AI lists three cases. 1 sale and 0 sales are edge cases: unusual answers that often break code.
She runs every case on the AI's code. Three sales give 14.00 and 4.67, a pass. One sale of 5.00 passes too.

visual.heading: Three cases on the AI's code
visual.label: Test

segments.say: So two cases pass. But the case that matters, 0 sales, fails.
The AI's code only works when there was nothing to fix.

messages.text: Code: my report with your check. Exact error: below. Expected result for 0 sales: No sales today. Actual result: it printed the heading, then the error report below. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

The cause is line 8. `sales >= 0` is true when sales is 0, so line 9 still divides by 0.
The smallest fix: `if sales > 0:`

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Now Asha writes the full debugging prompt: the code, the exact error, the expected result, no sales today, and the actual result, a crash.
She asks for the cause first. The AI names line 8: greater than or equal lets 0 through. The smallest fix is greater than 0.
Asha changes line 8 and runs it with 0. No sales today. No crash.
A fix can break a case that worked before. So she runs every case again. Three sales: still 14.00 and 4.67, and one sale still gives 5.00.

visual.heading: Every case again, on the fixed code
visual.label: Test

segments.say: All three cases pass on the fixed code.

visual.heading: Improve: easier to debug next time

messages.text: My report works. Suggest at most two changes that make future bugs easier to find, each with one reason. Do not change what it prints.

1. Rename `sale` to `sale_number`, so nobody adds it by mistake instead of `price`.
2. Keep a debug line inside the loop, so you can always see the total.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. The report works. Asha asks for at most two changes that make future bugs easier to find. And she adds: do not change what it prints.
Suggestion 1: rename sale to sale number, so nobody adds it instead of price. That would have made the bug from step 4 easier to spot!
Suggestion 2: keep a debug line inside the loop, so the total is always visible.

visual.heading: Testing suggestion 2
visual.hidden_text: Predict the change before the output appears.
visual.note: The user will type: 3, then 4.50, 6.00 and 3.50

segments.say: Asha tries both suggestions. Line 5 uses the new name.
And line 8 is the debug line the AI wants to keep.

ask.question: Asha said: do not change what it prints. Does suggestion 2 keep that promise?

after.say: No. Three extra debug lines appear in the report. The AI ignored her instruction.
Debug lines are for finding a bug, not for the finished report. So Asha keeps suggestion 1 only.

segments.say: Here is the result: a clear name on line 5, the check on line 8, and the same report as before. Every stage helped, and Asha checked every answer herself.

visual.question: An AI fixes your code and says it works now. What do you do next?
options: Trust it: it explained the fix
Run only the case that failed
Ask it if it is sure
Run the case that failed and the cases that worked
visual.explain: A fix can break something else. Test the failing case and the old cases.

segments.say: Quick check. An AI fixes your code, and says it works now. What do you do next?

after.say: D. Run the case that failed, and the cases that worked. A fix can break something else.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
Code, exact error, expected, actual.
After a fix, run every case again.

segments.say: Breather. Asha caught two AI mistakes: a check that let 0 through, and a change she did not ask for.
Next, mistakes beginners make while debugging.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 is a spot-it with Python's own suggestion. Mistake 3 is a spot-it on indentation. Mistake 4 is the decimal comma.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Line 3 should print the word Total and the value of total.

after.say: A comma between the two values. And look at the last line: Python even suggests it.
after.heading: Mistake 1: a missing comma

after.say: Python's suggestions are often right, so always read them.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: One more. Asha adds a debug line on line 5. Compare its start with line 4.

after.say: Line 5 has six spaces at the start, but the block uses four. Python reports an Indentation Error.
after.heading: Mistake 2: a debug line with the wrong indentation

after.say: The fix: indent a debug line exactly like the line above it.

segments.say: Mistake 3. In many countries, people write four and a half as 4 comma 50. Python accepts only a decimal point, so float stops with a Value Error.
The message even shows the exact text that failed. The fix: type 4 point 50.

items: Read Python's suggestions.
Create a variable before you use it.
Indent a debug line like its neighbours.

segments.say: Last breather. Now you know three mistakes that slow down a bug hunt.

items: Syntax error: nothing runs. Runtime error: a traceback partway. Logic error: a wrong result, no message.

segments.say: Let's recap. A syntax error stops everything. A runtime error stops partway. A logic error gives a wrong result, with no message.
Read a traceback from the bottom up. The line Python names is where it noticed, and the cause can be earlier.
Print debugging shows values while the program runs. And a debugging prompt has the code, the exact error, the expected result and the actual result.
And after a fix, test the case that failed, and the cases that worked.

visual.question: A program stops on line 12 with a `TypeError`. Where can the cause be?
options: Only on the last line of the file
On line 12 or on an earlier line
Nowhere: it is a mistake in Python
visual.explain: Line 12 is where Python noticed. A value can be wrong from an earlier line.

segments.say: One last check. A program stops on line 12 with a Type Error. Where can the cause be?

after.say: C. On line 12, or on an earlier line, like the cups from step 2.
